title: Here I Stand? The Diet of Worms, 1521
eyes: Frederick III ('the Wise'), Elector of Saxony
Johann von der Ecken (Johann Eck of Trier)
places: Worms, larger hall of the bishop's palace
Worms, residence of the Archbishop of Trier
The Ebernburg, Sickingen's castle near Bad Kreuznach, about 60 km from Worms
intro: On the evening of 18 April 1521, in a crowded and overheated hall of the bishop's palace at Worms, a 37-year-old friar already excommunicated by the pope refused before the 21-year-old emperor to retract his books. The scene became one of the founding images of modern Europe, and it was recorded at once by people with every reason to see it differently: the papal nuncio, the imperial examiner, the friar's own prince and his secretary, Venetian diplomats, and the friar himself. The record here is almost entirely letters, dispatches and official protocol rather than diaries, and the form tags say so. At its core are Girolamo Aleandro's dispatches to Rome, hostile and vivid; the imperial protocol of Johann von der Ecken's questions; Charles V's own declaration, written overnight in French; Luther's short letters before and after; and the reports of the Venetians Francesco Cornaro, who was at court during the hearings, and Gasparo Contarini, who arrived two days later and admitted he never saw Luther. Around them stand the English envoy Cuthbert Tunstall, the knight Ulrich von Hutten in a castle sixty kilometres away, the Spanish secretary Alfonso de Valdés, and Albrecht Dürer in Antwerp. The record is lopsided in a way readers should keep in view. Catholic voices at Worms were mostly diplomats writing to masters who wanted results, and Aleander in particular reported rumour as fact. Protestant memory, from the pamphlet printings of 1521 to the Table Talk of the 1530s, polished Luther's words and the journey into legend. Where the sources disagree, as on the last words of the speech, on the day Luther left, or on how long his safe conduct ran, both versions are given. The most famous words are the least certain. 'Here I stand, I can do no other' appears in the Wittenberg printing of the speech in 1521, but not in Spalatin's notes or in the earliest Latin Acta, which end with 'God help me, Amen'. Historians have argued both ways since the 1860s. Another celebrated line, the devils as many as roof tiles, comes from Luther's own later memories. A third has recently been questioned: the lament for Luther in Dürer's journal, which one scholar now attributes to an Antwerp friar. The chapter runs from the papal bull of June 1520 to the edict signed in the cathedral on 26 May 1521. In between come a hearing that was not a debate, a declaration of conscience on each side, three days of committee talks that went nowhere, and a staged kidnapping in the Thuringian Forest. The emperor kept his word on the safe conduct and then outlawed the man he had protected, and the man disappeared into a castle under a false name.

title: The House of Worship: Fatehpur Sikri, 1575–1582
places: near Bhera, on the Jhelum, Punjab
on the road north of Agra
Fatehpur Sikri, in the House of Worship in its early years
Agra–Fatehpur Sikri, then Gujarat in the 1580s
intro: In 1575 the Mughal emperor Akbar, then in his early thirties and master of most of northern India, had a hall built beside the mosque of his new red-sandstone city at Fatehpur Sikri. He called it the Ibadat Khana, the House of Worship. On Thursday nights, the eve of the Muslim Friday, he sat there with Sunni scholars, Sufi shaikhs, nobles and sayyids and put questions to them. Within four years the circle had widened to Shia scholars, Brahmans, Jain monks, Zoroastrian priests from Gujarat and, in February 1580, three Jesuits from Goa. Between 1579 and 1582 Akbar read the Friday sermon himself, received a signed decree from his ulama recognising his authority to choose between conflicting legal opinions, and finally drew a small circle of disciples into a devotional order of his own. Its nature is still argued over. This is a chapter built from chronicles and letters, not diaries, and the form tags say so. The Persian side is told by three court historians who knew each other well. Abu'l Fazl was Akbar's closest intellectual companion and wrote the official Akbarnama in the 1590s. Abd al-Qadir Badauni was a court scholar who took part in the early debates and came to hate where they led. He wrote his Muntakhab al-Tawarikh in secret, and it circulated only after Akbar's death. Nizamuddin Ahmad, Badauni's friend, wrote the Tabaqat-i Akbari, a dry official chronicle that says almost nothing about religion. The admirer and the critic often describe the same night in opposite terms. Here they are laid side by side and neither is treated as the truth. The European side comes from the Jesuits. Rodolfo Aquaviva, a 29-year-old Italian nobleman, wrote letters home from the court. The Catalan Antonio Monserrate kept notes that he later worked into a Latin Commentarius, finishing it in 1590–91 in captivity at Sanaa in Yemen. Francisco Henriques, a convert from Hormuz who spoke Persian, interpreted for them; he left no account of his own and is seen only through his companions. Monserrate also rode with Akbar's army on the 1581 campaign against Akbar's half-brother Mirza Hakim in Kabul, so the debates continued in camp. The Jesuits hoped to convert the emperor. Their accounts are as partisan as Badauni's, from the other side. Other voices reach the room only at second hand. The Jain teacher Hiravijaya Suri walked from Gujarat to Fatehpur Sikri around 1582–83, but his visit is known mainly from Sanskrit and Gujarati biographies written by his followers years later. The Parsi priest Dastur Meherji Rana of Navsari is known through his community's records and traditions. Shaikh Mubarak, the father of Abu'l Fazl and of the poet Faizi, drafted the 1579 decree. Birbal, the Brahman courtier of later legend, appears here only where the chronicles name him. Akbar himself wrote nothing that survives. He speaks through his farmans (imperial orders) and through what others report he said. The convergences are the sessions and turning points several of these people recorded

title: The Long Room: Philadelphia, Summer 1787
places: A seat in front of the presiding chair in the Assembly Room of the State House
The President's chair on the dais
The secretary's table in the Assembly Room
The New York bench, beside Hamilton and John Lansing
The Georgia bench, 31 May to about 1 July
The Pennsylvania bench, carried to the State House in a sedan chair
Philadelphia lodgings and Franklin's garden, a short walk from the State House
The Maryland bench, 9 June to 4 September
intro: For sixteen weeks in the summer of 1787, about fifty-five men met behind closed doors in the Assembly Room of the Pennsylvania State House. They had been sent to amend the Articles of Confederation and wrote a new constitution instead. Their first rules forbade printing or repeating anything said in the room, and the rule held: the public saw nothing until the finished text appeared in the Pennsylvania Packet on 19 September. So the room is known almost entirely through private papers, and the form tags say so. Only the secretary, William Jackson, kept an official Journal, and it records motions and state votes, never a speech. Everything else comes from delegates' notes (Madison, Yates, King, McHenry, Pierce, Paterson, Hamilton), letters home (Mason, Gerry, Washington, Hamilton), Washington's spare diary, Franklin's written speeches, and a visitor's journal (Cutler). Some of this reached print generations later and through interested hands: the Journal in 1819, Yates in 1821 in an edition shaped by Madison's enemies, Madison's own notes in 1840 after decades of revision. Each eye's authenticity note says how far to trust it. The arc is a series of votes. On 29 May the Virginia Plan proposed a national government apportioned by population. On 15 June Paterson's New Jersey Plan defended one state, one vote, and lost on 19 June. On 18 June Hamilton argued for going much further. Through late June and early July the Convention deadlocked, with Franklin asking for prayers on 28 June and a tie on 2 July. On 16 July the Connecticut, or Great, Compromise carried by a single state: population in the House, equality in the Senate. Slavery ran through the whole summer. It was there in the three-fifths ratio adopted on 11 June, in Gouverneur Morris's attack on it on 8 August, and in the slave-trade week of 21–25 August that ended with imports protected until 1808. A navigation-act bargain followed, and a fugitive clause was added on 29 August. These debates are given as the delegates spoke and voted, from Madison's notes and Martin's later report. No enslaved or free Black person was in the room. The Pennsylvania Abolition Society's memorial of 2 June asking the Convention to suppress the trade was left with Franklin, its president, and there is no record it was ever presented. The chapter ends with the signing on 17 September: Franklin's speech, read by Wilson, his remark about the rising sun, Washington's one speech and his dinner at the City Tavern, and the three who refused, Randolph, Mason and Gerry. It closes on the first Federalist essay of 27 October, and on Luther Martin's November report to Maryland, which broke the secrecy to argue the other side.

title: The Congress Dances: Vienna, 1814–1815
eyes: Franz, Baron Hager von Allentsteig (Austrian Polizeihofstelle)
places: Conference of the eight powers, Vienna
Vienna's ballrooms, theatres and the Prince de Ligne's house
intro: In the autumn of 1814 the victors over Napoleon gathered in Vienna to redraw the map of Europe. The Emperor of Russia and the King of Prussia rode into the city on 25 September; behind them came ministers, princes of defunct states, petitioners for cities, churches, Jewish communities and booksellers, and a crowd of hostesses, artists and spies. The Congress as a plenary assembly never met. The decisions were made in small rooms by five or so ministers, and announced in protocols drafted by a secretary. This chapter lays those rooms beside the paper that came out of them. Talleyrand's letters to Louis XVIII are the backbone: he wrote almost daily, from the September conference where he objected to the word 'allies' to the signing of the Final Act. Around him stand Metternich, the host; Castlereagh and then Wellington for Britain; Hardenberg and Wilhelm von Humboldt for Prussia; and Tsar Alexander, who kept no diary and appears only in what others reported he said. Friedrich von Gentz, the secretary, kept a private diary whose verdicts are blunter than the minutes he wrote. Other eyes watched from outside. Baron Hager's police agents copied embassy papers and noted who dined with whom, for Emperor Francis to read each morning. The comte de La Garde-Chambonas, a guest in the ballrooms, wrote years later the memoir that gave the Congress its reputation for dancing. Cardinal Consalvi petitioned for the Pope's lost provinces. In London, Wilberforce and the abolitionists waited for a condemnation of the slave trade; in Paris, and then in exile at Ghent, Louis XVIII read his minister's despatches. The honest record here is mostly letters, despatches, police reports and parliamentary records, with one true diary (Gentz's) and two memoirs written later (Metternich's and La Garde's), which are flagged. Each eye wrote for a reader: Talleyrand for a king and the postal censors, Castlereagh for a cabinet and Parliament, the police for an emperor. On Poland and Saxony the positions are given as each side stated them: Russia's claim to a Polish kingdom under the Tsar, Prussia's claim to Saxony as its promised reward, and the Austrian, British and French arguments for the balance of power and for the Saxon king's legitimacy. The slave-trade declaration of 8 February 1815 is reported for what it said and did not do: the powers condemned the trade in principle, but left each state to fix its own date and set up no enforcement. Within a month the news that Napoleon had left Elba reached Vienna (7 March); on 13 March the powers declared him outside the law. The Final Act was signed on 9 June, nine days before Waterloo.

title: The Wesleyan Chapel: Seneca Falls, July 1848
eyes: Report of the Woman's Rights Convention (the printed Proceedings)
Minutes of the Rochester Woman's Rights Convention (secretaries)
The newspapers (Courier, Tribune, Herald, Oneida Whig, Mechanic's Advocate, Public Ledger)
places: Freemasons' Hall, Great Queen Street, London
Came by wagon from near Waterloo
The chair of the Unitarian Church, Rochester
Seneca Falls, New York City, Utica, Albany, Philadelphia
intro: In June 1840 the World Anti-Slavery Convention met in London, and the American women sent as delegates were not allowed to take their seats. Lucretia Mott, a Philadelphia Quaker minister, recorded the exclusion in her travel diary in plain Quaker dating. Elizabeth Cady Stanton, a 24-year-old bride on her honeymoon, sat beside her as a spectator. Forty years later Stanton named that week as the beginning of the women's rights movement. Eight years later, on 9 July 1848, five women met for tea at Jane Hunt's house outside Waterloo, New York, and decided to call a convention. They gave the public less than ten days' notice. On 16 July they drafted a Declaration of Sentiments at the M'Clintock family's parlour table, modelling it on the Declaration of Independence. On 19 and 20 July some three hundred people came to the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls. The Declaration was adopted unanimously. A resolution claiming the vote was contested, and later accounts say Frederick Douglass spoke to carry it. One hundred people signed: 68 women, and 32 men listed as 'present in favor of the movement'. This room has an official record. The printed Report is the organisers' own minutes, and it is laid here beside dated letters, Douglass's editorial, the newspapers that reprinted and mocked the Declaration, and the minutes of the adjourned meeting at Rochester on 2 August, where Abigail Bush became one of the first women to preside over a mixed public meeting. The record is mostly letters, printed proceedings and newspapers rather than diaries. Much of the best-known detail comes from memoirs written decades later: Stanton's History of Woman Suffrage (1881) and Eighty Years and More (1898), and the recollections of the signers Charlotte Woodward and Rhoda Palmer. Those entries are marked as later accounts. The press is reported here as it wrote. The Tribune printed the news straight, the Herald reprinted the Declaration, and upstate and Philadelphia papers ridiculed it. Stanton later wrote that many signers withdrew their names. The chapter ends at Worcester in October 1850, where the first national women's rights convention drew delegates from eleven states. Mott and Douglass were in the hall, and Stanton sent a letter.

title: Paris, 1919: The Peace Conference and Those Outside the Door
eyes: Nguyen Ai Quoc (later Ho Chi Minh)
places: Hôtel Crillon, League of Nations Commission
His residence at 11 Place des États-Unis, the Quai d'Orsay and the Hôtel Crillon
Hôtel Crillon, Place de la Concorde
Hotel Bristol, rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré
Hôtel Continental and the Quai d'Orsay
intro: On 18 January 1919 delegates from some thirty states gathered at the French Foreign Ministry on the Quai d'Orsay to make the peace after the First World War. Within days the real work had passed to a Council of Ten, two leaders from each of the five great powers, and from late March to a Council of Four: Wilson, Lloyd George, Clemenceau and Orlando, meeting in Wilson's study with an interpreter and, later, one secretary. Everything else was outside the door. This chapter lays the official record beside the private one. The minutes of the Council of Ten and the plenary sessions printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, and Paul Mantoux's interpreter's notes of the Four, give what was said in the room as secretaries summarised it. Around them stand the diaries and dated memoranda of those close to it: Colonel House, the sidelined Secretary of State Lansing, Wilson's doctor Grayson, Lloyd George's secretary Frances Stevenson, the young diplomat Harold Nicolson. Several eyes left no diary at all, only speeches, memoranda and petitions, and the form tags say so. The room heard claims that could not all be satisfied. China and Japan both claimed the German rights in Shandong. The Emir Faisal asked independence for the Arab lands of Asia while France pointed to its wartime agreements and a French-backed Central Syrian Committee put its own case to the Council of Ten on 13 February; on 27 February the Zionist delegation of Weizmann, Sokolow and Ussishkin was heard on Palestine. Japan asked for a clause on racial equality, and won a majority that the chair ruled insufficient. Germany was summoned in May to receive the terms, not to negotiate them. The chapter reports what each side said and decided, with the evidence, and gives no verdicts. Some of the most consequential people in Paris that year never got into the room. W. E. B. Du Bois convened a Pan-African Congress at the Grand Hôtel in February. A young Vietnamese who signed himself Nguyen Ai Quoc sent the delegations eight modest demands in June. In Beijing, on 4 May, students marched against the Shandong decision. Their papers sit in the American delegation's files, received and unanswered. Most of the private sources here were first published after 1928 (Nicolson in 1933, Stevenson in 1971, Mantoux in 1955, Koo's oral history decades later), so they are summarised, not quoted. Short quotations come only from English texts published before 1929, chiefly Lansing's 1921 memoir, House's papers as printed in 1928 and The Crisis, and from US government records within twelve words.

title: Yalta, February 1945
places: Malta, HMS Orion in Grand Harbour
Livadia Palace, the former Romanov summer palace, where all eight plenary sessions met
Vorontsov Palace, Alupka, about 12 miles west of Livadia
Vorontsov Palace, with the Prime Minister's party
Livadia Palace, which she helped prepare
intro: In the first days of February 1945 the leaders of the three largest Allied powers met in palaces on the southern coast of the Crimea, a territory that German forces had left only nine months earlier. The Red Army was on the Oder; the Western armies had just turned back the Ardennes offensive; the war with Japan looked set to last into 1946 or beyond. Over eight plenary sessions at the Livadia Palace (4–11 February), with foreign ministers and chiefs of staff meeting in parallel at the Yusupov and Vorontsov palaces, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin argued over the fate of Germany, the government and frontiers of Poland, the voting rules of a new world organisation, and the terms on which the Soviet Union would join the war in the Pacific. The room itself left an unusual record. There was no single stenographic transcript. The American minutes by Charles Bohlen, who interpreted for Roosevelt and wrote at the same time, together with the pencilled notes of H. Freeman Matthews and Alger Hiss, were published by the State Department in 1955 in the middle of a fierce domestic argument over the conference. The British and Soviet records are separate and selective; the Soviet record appeared much later. Stalin and Roosevelt kept no diaries, so both speak here only through others' minutes and their own public words. Around that record this chapter lays the private writing of people who were in the palaces but mostly outside the conference room: Churchill's doctor, whose 'diary' was rewritten for publication; the Foreign Office's senior official writing to his wife; and the three daughters, Sarah Churchill, Anna Roosevelt Boettiger and Kathleen Harriman, whose letters and diary describe looted palaces, ruined Sevastopol, champagne at breakfast and fathers worn down by the sessions. Several eyes survive only as later books or recollections (Stettinius 1949, Byrnes 1947, Lunghi 1996 and 2007), and are marked so. The conference produced public decisions (a Declaration on Liberated Europe, a formula for a reorganised Polish government pledged to free elections, zones and a reparations commission for Germany, a date for the San Francisco conference) and a secret one (the agreement on Soviet entry into the war with Japan in return for territory and rights in the Far East, signed without China's knowledge). Outside the room stood the Polish government-in-exile in London, which had not been consulted and rejected the decisions on Poland within two days. Yalta has been argued over ever since. To some it was a realistic settlement that recognised where armies already stood and secured Soviet commitments to elections, the United Nations and the Pacific war; to others, especially in Poland and among Cold War critics in the United States, it was a betrayal that handed Eastern Europe to Soviet control. The diarists themselves already disagreed. This chapter reports what each side said, wrote and signed, and leaves the verdict to the reader.

title: Bandung, April 1955
places: South China Sea, off the Natuna Islands
Luncheon of the Colombo powers, China, the Philippines and Thailand, Bandung
The Chinese delegation's villa and the conference halls, Bandung
intro: In April 1955 the delegations of twenty-nine Asian and African governments met in a converted colonial club in Bandung, West Java, renamed Gedung Merdeka, the Freedom Building, for the week. Five prime ministers had called them there: Nehru of India, Kotelawala of Ceylon, U Nu of Burma, Mohammad Ali of Pakistan and Ali Sastroamidjojo of Indonesia, who had met at Bogor at the end of December 1954. They invited the People's Republic of China, Japan, Egypt and the new or nearly new states of the Middle East, South and Southeast Asia and Africa; they did not invite Israel, South Africa, Taiwan or either Korea. Roughly half the delegations came from governments aligned with the West, several of them bound by treaty to the United States or Britain, a few from communist states, and the rest from governments trying to stay outside both blocs. No European or American government sat in the room, and that was the point. Washington watched by telegram, briefing its friends while saying in public that the meeting was none of its concern. The People's Republic came under a shadow: on 11 April the Kashmir Princess, an Air India charter carrying members of the Chinese delegation and journalists, was destroyed by a bomb over the South China Sea. Zhou Enlai was not aboard. Beijing blamed American and Nationalist Chinese agents; Taipei denied it; the Hong Kong police later named a suspect who had fled to Taiwan. This chapter reports those positions and the inquiries without deciding between them. The private record of the room is thin. The Political Committee, where the real arguments happened, met in closed session, and no delegate's diary of the week has been published. What survives are speeches printed by the host government, the Chinese delegation's hour-by-hour cables to Beijing, Nehru's dated letters and notes to India's chief ministers, the American ambassador's telegrams and the Secretary of State's briefings, and the work of the people outside the door: the African American correspondent Ethel Payne, the novelist Richard Wright, Congressman Adam Clayton Powell Jr., and the China specialist A. Doak Barnett, who reconstructed the closed sessions from lobby briefings. Several of the most quoted accounts, by Kotelawala, Romulo and Wright, were written a year later, and they are marked as such. The week's arguments were about words. Was Soviet rule in Eastern Europe colonialism, as Kotelawala insisted on 21 April? Should new states join military pacts, as Turkey, Pakistan and the Philippines had, or keep out, as Nehru argued? Could communist China be trusted by its neighbours? The answers came as phrases: Zhou's offer to seek common ground, colonialism 'in all its manifestations', and ten principles that put racial equality and non-interference beside the right of collective self-defence. Every eye here read those phrases differently, and the differences are the chapter.
